column9: Isaiah 3:10; Chagigah 12a. English translation of source: “Isaiah 3:10: ‘Say of the righteous that it shall be good, for they will eat the fruit of their deeds.’ Chagigah 12a: ‘Rabbi Elazar said: By the light that the Holy One, blessed be He, created on the first day, Adam could look from one end of the world to the other. When the Holy One saw the generation of the Flood and the generation of the Dispersion, and saw that their deeds were corrupt, He arose and concealed it from them, as it says, ‘Their light is withheld from the wicked’ [Job 38:15]. For whom did He conceal it? For the righteous in the future, as it says, ‘God saw that the light was good’; and ‘good’ means the righteous, as it says, ‘Say of the righteous that it is good.’’” Context and connection: The link is pivotal for Rav Tzadok: the flood generation’s failure entails loss of access to this higher light, but the righteous person who preserves the covenant becomes a vessel for it. The discussion of the second day’s missing ‘good’ is a related midrashic theme rather than the main argument of Chagigah 12a.
column11: Connection to this footnote: This closely parallels the notion that the primordial light is preserved for the righteous and is unveiled through spiritual refinement.
column13: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Machshavot Charutz 0-9:8 (§4): “For every reality divides into ten, which is the measure of a complete spiritual stature. And just as across the entire stature of evil the beginning is arrogance (the Crown) and the end is lust (the feminine/Nukva); so within the stature of lust itself, its root and inception whence flows the entire structure is pride, the craving for self-exaltation; this being the final crown among the ten crowns of impurity of the root of defilement; its first crown being the primordial arrogance of "and you shall be as gods" spoken by the Serpent, and its final crown being the lust for personal aggrandizement.” Connection to this note: In Machshavot Charutz 0-9:8 (§4), Rav Tzadok develops the parallel foundation illuminating Exodus 12:2 and the teaching in Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom.

column9: Niddah 13b; Genesis 38:9–10. English translation of source: “Niddah 13b: ‘The Sages taught: Converts and those who ‘play with children’ delay the Messiah. ... But what does ‘those who play with children’ mean? If it refers to intercourse between males, those who do so are liable to stoning! Rather, [the discussion concerns] intercourse by way of other limbs, and these are ‘people of the Flood.’’ Genesis 38:9–10: ‘Onan knew that the offspring would not be his. When he came to his brother’s wife, he wasted [his seed] upon the ground so as not to give offspring to his brother. What he did was evil in the eyes of the Lord, and He put him to death also.’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok invokes the Flood generation as the paradigmatic corruption of the covenantal power of yesod. The source supplies the severity of the comparison; his further connection of the generation’s failing to the sixth day, the sixth millennium and the spiritual work of restoration is an interpretive expansion.
column11: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Tzidkat HaTzadik 96: “One who guards the Covenant and never experienced a nocturnal emission in his days is termed "fair of form" (yefeh to'ar) in Scripture, as in the case of Joseph: "fair of form" (Genesis 39:6); and regarding this it is said: "Grace is deceitful and beauty is vain" (Proverbs 31:30), for we find even among gentile nations those who were clean of this, such as Og who escaped from the Generation of the Flood, and that without an ark at all; surely a miracle would not occur for falsehood, but rather he was not subject to the Flood decree because he did not spill seed, as written in Niddah 13b.” Connection to this note: In Tzidkat HaTzadik 96, Rav Tzadok develops the parallel foundation illuminating Exodus 12:2 and the teaching in Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom.
column13: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 41:18–21: “Adam bound them to their root, revealing why they were created; vegetation not receiving names because it was on a lower plane, requiring elevation through human consumption into the human form. Yet in the Flood generation all flesh corrupted its way, mixing roots until animals lost awareness of their origin; whereupon all animals consented to be elevated through human eating into the human form, ascending to a higher spiritual plane.” Connection to this note: This Beis Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 41:18–21 sheds direct light on Exodus 12:2 and Rav Tzadok's exposition in Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom.

column9: Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 16; Genesis 11:1. English translation of source: “‘Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: They instituted the joining of courtyards [eiruvei chatzeiros] only for the sake of peace. How so? A woman sends her son to her neighbor, and the neighbor bends down and kisses him. His mother says: ‘She truly loves him,’ and affection for her enters her heart; thus, through the eiruv, they make peace. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: ‘I make peace in My world, but these wicked ones are setting out to bring strife into the world.’ How do we know that they disputed with the Holy One? From the verse that begins the matter: ‘And the whole earth was of one language and of united words’ [Genesis 11:1].’” Context and connection: An eruv makes distinct homes function cooperatively; the word itself suggests joining. But the Midrash shows why uniform language and collective effort are not sufficient. Rav Tzadok contrasts unity ordered toward Hashem’s peace with an alliance organized around rebellion.
column10: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 1:3 (§2)
column11: Connection to this footnote: This source interprets the dispersion of the Generation of the Dispersion through the distinction between destructive and holy unity.
column13: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 1:3 (§2): “And one who does not believe this—no commandments or admonitions will avail him, for such is a root bearing gall, his essence not partaking of the holiness of Israel at all, Israel's primary fountainhead and life-force being the divine utterance of "I am Hashem." Therefore this is not an ordinary commandment enacted through effort from below, but a primordial gift from above without lower awakening, their very spiritual root being constituted thus.” Connection to this note: In Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 1:3 (§2), Rav Tzadok develops the parallel foundation illuminating Exodus 12:2 and the teaching in Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom.

column9: Sanhedrin 71b. English translation of source: “‘The wine and sleep of the wicked are good for them and good for the world; the wine and sleep of the righteous are bad for them and bad for the world. The dispersal of the wicked is good for them and good for the world; the dispersal of the righteous is bad for them and bad for the world. The gathering of the wicked is bad for them and bad for the world; the gathering of the righteous is good for them and good for the world.’” Context and connection: The same social phenomenon—people coming together—can bring blessing or destruction, depending on the moral character and purpose of the assembly. Rav Tzadok uses the principle to explain why the apparent solidarity of the Tower generation was not the unity of holiness.
column11: Connection to this footnote: It further distinguishes outward togetherness from gathering around a corrupt purpose; collective strength is not inherently sanctified.
column13: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Poked Akarim 4:21 (§6): “And even though his son Manasseh was wicked, from him descended a dynasty of righteous kings, Mashiach issuing from his seed; wherefore whatever Hashem bestows on His own is certainly good. And when praying for children, one must pray for righteous sons and Torah scholars, through whom the glory of Heaven is magnified, sanctified, and increased [and I heard that this is the essence of the Kaddish recited by a son for his father: "May His great Name be magnified...", declaring that his father's purpose in procreation was that His Name be magnified, siring souls in Israel who sanctify His Name.” Connection to this note: In Poked Akarim 4:21 (§6), Rav Tzadok develops the parallel foundation illuminating Exodus 12:2 and the teaching in Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom.

column9: Genesis 1:31; Bereishis Rabbah 9. English translation of source: “Genesis 1:31: ‘God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning—the sixth day.’ Bereishis Rabbah 9: ‘Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: ‘Behold, it was very good’—this refers to this world; ‘behold, it was very good’—this refers to the World to Come; the Holy One looked at both in one glance.’ Another teaching says: ‘ ‘Behold, it was very good’—this is the good inclination; ‘behold, it was very good’—this is the evil inclination. But is the evil inclination very good? If not for the evil inclination, a person would not build a house, marry, beget children, or engage in business.’” Context and connection: For Rav Tzadok, the sixth day corresponds to yesod, the power that should direct physical desire toward covenantal holiness. Its repair involves bringing even forces that have been diverted from the good back into their proper order. The identification of the sixth day with yesod is his mystical interpretation.
column11: Connection to this footnote: This is an unusually close interpretation of the same Midrash in relation to Noach’s generation and the restoration of “very good.”
column13: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Takanat HaShavin 15:103 (§2): “And this derives from the root of the living soul in man in holiness, through the droplet of bile that appeases and checks the fury of the liver. Bereishis Rabbah 9:7 — “ve-hinneh tov me’od — this is the evil inclination [yetzer ha-ra].” R’ Nachman expounds that were it not for the yetzer, no man would build a house, marry, beget children, or engage in commerce. This grounds R’ Tzadok’s point that the very drives of anger and desire were “very good” as implanted for sustaining life and perpetuating the species — evil only in their misuse.” Connection to this note: In Takanat HaShavin 15:103 (§2), Rav Tzadok develops the parallel foundation illuminating Exodus 12:2 and the teaching in Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom.

column9: Rosh Hashanah 18a; I Samuel 3:14. English translation of source: “‘Rava said: ‘By sacrifice and by meal-offering [the sin of Eli’s household] is not atoned’—but it is atoned by Torah. Abaye said: ‘By sacrifice and by meal-offering it is not atoned’—but it is atoned by Torah and acts of lovingkindness. Rabba and Abaye were descendants of the house of Eli: Rabba, who engaged in Torah, lived forty years; Abaye, who engaged in Torah and lovingkindness, lived sixty years.’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok cites the passage because it distinguishes an ordinary route to atonement from a higher one that still remains open. His parallel is that some forms of spiritual damage require Torah’s transformative wisdom rather than merely the familiar modes of repentance.
column11: Connection to this footnote: The passage shows how even one who has fallen deeply can be transformed through powerful longing and repentance.
column12: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach 8:4
column13: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach 8:4: “Even though he had already fathered a son, therefore it is fitting to remain involved with the father. Because “Noach was a righteous man [Tsaddik],” and still has a connection to his father. However, with the ten generations from Noach until Avraham, it does not say “and all his days were,” for Avraham Avinu was a sage in words of Torah, as we say that he fulfilled the entire Torah before it was given.” Connection to this note: This Beis Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach 8:4 sheds direct light on Exodus 12:2 and Rav Tzadok's exposition in Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom.

column9: Proverbs 4:20–22. English translation of source: “‘My son, give attention to my words; incline your ear to my sayings. Do not let them depart from your eyes; keep them within your heart. For they are life to those who find them, and healing to all their flesh.’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok stresses the final phrase: Torah is not presented merely as a remedy for one isolated fault. By illuminating the heart and directing a person’s life, it offers the possibility of a healing that reaches through all the faculties affected by the original blemish.
column11: Connection to this footnote: This Midrash as quoted and expounded by Shem MiShmuel directly joins attention to Torah with life and healing, the theme of the Proverbs verses.
column12: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Leviticus, Kedoshim 4
column13: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Leviticus, Kedoshim 4: ““You shall be holy” (Leviticus 19:2): in Vayikra Rabbah 24:6 our Sages taught, “Wherever you find a protective fence against immorality (geder ervah), you find holiness.” Every superfluous craving for the indulgences of this world is a form of nakedness (ervat ha-aretz); whoever erects a firm inner fence to guard his eyes and heart merits the resting of supernal kedushah.” Connection to this note: This Beis Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Leviticus, Kedoshim 4 sheds direct light on Exodus 12:2 and Rav Tzadok's exposition in Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom.

column9: Psalms 97:11. English translation of source: “‘Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for those whose hearts are upright.’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok understands the righteous, particularly the person who guards the covenant and resists the yetzer, as fit to receive a higher light. He links this sown light to supernal wisdom and Written Torah; the verse supports the theme of promised illumination, while that specific Torah-mapping comes from his exposition.
column11: Connection to this footnote: The concealed light is described as available to the righteous across the generations and as manifest especially on holy days.
column13: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 65:58–60: “And because Adam encompassed all generations to come, he experienced all future illuminations and all dark concealments destined for his children. Thus he tasted the very concealment of Haman's era when asked “Hamin ha-etz” (see section 60). Yet God also balanced this: in every generation, despite deep darkness, Hashem shines courage from the realization that we are His handiwork.” Connection to this note: This Beis Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 65:58–60 sheds direct light on Exodus 12:2 and Rav Tzadok's exposition in Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom.

column9: Taanit 15a; Psalms 97:11. English translation of source: “‘Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: I too say that not everyone [is destined] for light, and not everyone for gladness. The righteous are [destined] for light, and the upright for gladness. The righteous for light, as it says, ‘Light is sown for the righteous’; and the upright for gladness, as it says, ‘And for the upright of heart, gladness’ [Psalm 97:11].’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok employs this rabbinic pairing to distinguish the revelation of higher light through Written Torah from the illuminating delight of Oral Torah, which straightens understanding and the heart. This identification of the two Torah dimensions is his own interpretive continuation.
column11: Connection to this footnote: The statement directly connects the Shabbos lamp to the primordial light reserved for the righteous.
column13: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Likkutei Maamarim 1-16:40 (§3): “And this generates supreme joy. And as written in Ta'anit (15a): “Not all merit light, and not all merit joy; rather the righteous (tzaddikim) are destined for light, and the upright (yesharim) are destined for joy, as it is said: ‘Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart’ (Psalms 97:11).” And a 'tzaddik' is one who restrains and subdues his passions, and he abides without such overt exuberant joy, meriting only 'light'—which is Torah, which is an internalized spiritual perception.” Connection to this note: In Likkutei Maamarim 1-16:40 (§3), Rav Tzadok develops the parallel foundation illuminating Exodus 12:2 and the teaching in Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom.

column4: Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom
column9: Proverbs 13:9. English translation of source: “‘The light of the righteous rejoices, but the lamp of the wicked is extinguished.’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok joins this verse to Tehillim’s ‘Light is sown for the righteous.’ Together they show both a light bestowed from above and a light that grows into joy through the right ordering of the heart. In his reading, this points to the relationship between Written and Oral Torah.
column11: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Et HaOchel 10 (§7): “And the Plague of the Firstborn corresponds to the commandment "I am [Hashem your God]," which is the root of all, while Egypt was the root of evil; and therefore at the time of the Plague of the Firstborn, Israel ate the Pesach offering, matzah, and maror to rectify all categories of eating, and the root was rectified for good; and it is said: "no stranger shall eat thereof" [Exodus 12:43], which our Sages expounded: "yet he eats of matzah and maror," which is designed to provide rectifications even for deniers, since "even though he has sinned, he remains an Israelite."” Connection to this note: In Et HaOchel 10 (§7), Rav Tzadok develops the parallel foundation illuminating Exodus 12:2 and the teaching in Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom.
column13: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Tiferet Yosef, Noach 1:3: “For prior to Noah, existence was still within the state of the “worlds that were destroyed” (almin de-itcharavu). And as we see, previously it is written (Genesis 4:1-2): “and she bore Cain... and she bore further his brother Abel” — where there was as yet no cohesion or connection between one and the other; whereas from Noah onward the World of Rectification began, and here it is written: “Shem, Ham, and Japheth” [linked together with the connecting 'vav' and direct accusatives], indicating that they possessed mutual connection and integration.” Connection to this note: This Beis Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Tiferet Yosef, Noach 1:3 sheds direct light on Exodus 12:2 and Rav Tzadok's exposition in Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom.

column4: Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom
column9: Genesis 7:11. English translation of source: “‘In the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month—on that very day all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the windows of heaven were opened.’” Context and connection: The Zohar makes the year-number a symbolic sign for the sixth millennium: earthly wellsprings and heavenly openings correspond to different manifestations of wisdom. Rav Tzadok’s reading reverses the Flood’s destructive imagery into the possibility of a new release of Torah illumination capable of helping a person return.
column11: Connection to this footnote: This supplies a distinct Chassidic reading of the Flood waters as a process of purification, not only destruction.
column13: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Machshavot Charutz 0-8:14 (§3): “Through Eliyahu who turns the heart of children to their fathers and unifies all souls within their Source; and through this the whole world is rectified, man being a microcosm encompassing the universe; and even the animal soul is elevated through its integration within the human soul; and through this Israel are severed from the idolaters who embody the animal soul severed from the divine human soul.” Connection to this note: In Machshavot Charutz 0-8:14 (§3), Rav Tzadok develops the parallel foundation illuminating Exodus 12:2 and the teaching in Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom.

column4: Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom
column9: Genesis 6:9. English translation of source: “‘These are the generations of Noah: Noah was a righteous man, wholehearted in his generations; Noah walked with God.’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok gives ‘righteous’ its further kabbalistic force: the tzaddik is connected with yesod, the covenantal foundation. Because Noach resisted his generation’s corruption, the six-hundredth year of his life becomes an apt symbolic marker for the point called yesod within yesod.
column10: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 7:3 (§2)
column11: Connection to this footnote: The correspondence between Noach and Shabbos deepens the Torah’s description of him as a righteous person and a source of rest.
column13: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 7:3 (§2): “This redemption issuing from their pedigree, their intrinsic root being good and holy, as elucidated above several times. column9: Zohar, Pinchas 10:58-12:70: “In the Zohar (Pinchas, Ra’aya Meheimna III 216b), it is further expounded that in the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, when the fountains of the great deep and the windows of heaven opened, the soul of Moses was ready to draw down the Written and Oral Torah as waters of blessing, but because the generation spurned God’s ways, those waters turned into the judgment of the Flood.” Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Pinchas 10:58-12:70) to illuminate his statement here (“who was present then, as stated in Ra'aya Meheimna (Zohar Part III, 216b); yet the Generation of the Flood refused to receive it, and as written (Shemot Rabbah, Parashah 30) on the verse ‘And the knowledge of Your...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: I dreamed [while residing in Izbica] that they were revealing to me certain matters concerning the root of my soul, and among those disclosures they were telling me that the generation of Mashiach will be the very same souls as the Generation of the Wilderness [and Mashiach embodies the soul of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, as cited in Raya Mehemna (Zohar III, 246b)], and they themselves are the selfsame souls as the Generation of the Flood [for Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, was also present there, as taught in the Zohar (III, 216b) and stated in Chullin 139b: "for that he also (beshagam)" equals the gematria of Moses (345)].
column13: And therefore Hashem does not judge man for future deeds, even though He foresees all, because for the present no portal of sin has opened within him. Thus Noah was saved from the Flood, but had to flee into the Ark; for one who is completely pure and righteous needs no ark, deliverance standing abundant before Hashem, just as Moses and all who went out of Egypt walked in the midst of the sea on dry ground, requiring no ark.

When a judge sits and judges truthfully, the Holy One blessed be He forsakes the heavens of heavens, as it were, and rests His Divine…’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Shemot Rabbah 30) to illuminate his statement here (“and as written (Shemot Rabbah, Parashah 30) on the verse ‘And the knowledge of Your ways we do not desire’—this is Torah. Therefore it was hinted: ‘all the fountains of the great deep burst open’, which alludes to...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.

This way is thus compared to a hedge of thorns, for the heart cannot be free of thoughts and desires even for a moment. Then once desire is removed from the heart, thoughts of anger and the like enter in, and in this way the whole way becomes like a hedge of thorns.

column9: Zohar I, Vayeira 117a (conclusion as preserved in Pri Tzaddik). English translation of source: “‘In the six-hundredth year of the sixth [millennium], the gates of wisdom above will open, and the springs of wisdom below, and the world will be readied to enter into the seventh, like a person preparing on the sixth day, once the sun has begun to set, to enter into Shabbos. So too [with the world]. And your sign is: ‘In the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life ... all the fountains of the great deep burst open’ [Genesis 7:11].’” Context and connection: The sequence of images is essential: opening wisdom is preparation for a sanctified seventh period, not an end in itself. Rav Tzadok interprets the number six hundred through the six middos and the human task of refining desire; the final approach to Shabbos denotes a divine completion beyond human effort. The wording follows the excerpt in Pri Tzaddik because Zohar editions use differing foliation.
column11: Connection to this footnote: The sixth millennium prepares and gathers the many partial acts of repair into the wholeness of the seventh, complementing Rav Tzadok’s concluding account of the opened gates of wisdom.
column13: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Yisrael Kedoshim 0-8:1 (§9): “And even transgressors receive according to their inborn ancestral root which can never be severed completely by sin; yet that light is progressively diminished through sins, the supernal inspiration from Above perpetually matching the sanctification from below!” Connection to this note: In Yisrael Kedoshim 0-8:1 (§9), Rav Tzadok develops the parallel foundation illuminating Exodus 12:2 and the teaching in Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom.

One interpretation says that 'good man' is the Holy One, blessed be He;...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: And although it is human nature as well that if an offender expresses remorse and seeks forgiveness one should pardon and not be cruel, and the attribute of Justice is not cruelty, Heaven forbid, but fair, equitable judgment; yet that applies only when the offender himself initiates remorse and repentance; whereas for the Supreme Sovereign to come seeking out the rebel, urging him to request pardon— this is certainly unlike human conduct and transcends standard judicial procedure.

column13: “And Korach took .…” (Bamidbar, 16:1)The Midrash (in Bamidbar Rabba, Korach, 18:17) tells us, “he saw the great chain of generations that would come out of him.” Since he saw this he became arrogant, daring to believe that surely he was the greatest of God’s servants. Of this it is said (Mishlei, 27:1), “Do not boast of tomorrow, for you don’t know what the day may bring forth.”

column4: Peri Tzadik, Noach 10 — The Haftarah of Noach and the Power of Intercession / Motzaei Shabbat: Eliyahu and the Hope of Redemption
column9: Bereshit Rabbah 12:9: ‘Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa said: “When they were created [behibare’am]” – be’Avraham and be’Avraham are spelled with the same letters. – due to the merit of Abraham. Rabbi Azarya said regarding this statement of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa: “You alone are the Lord; You made [the heavens, the heaven of heavens, and all their host, the earth and everything that is on it, the seas] and everything that is in them” (Nehemiah 9:6). And for what purpose was all this effort undertaken? It is for: “You are the Lord, the God who chose Abram, and took him out of Ur of the Chaldeans, and set his name as Abraham” (Nehemiah 9:7). Rabbi Yudan said: “The ibex are in the high mountains” is not written here,…’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Noach 10 — The Haftarah of Noach and the Power of Intercession / Motzaei Shabbat: Eliyahu and the Hope of Redemption, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 12:9) to illuminate his statement here (“and expounded (Bereishit Rabbah 12:9): ‘in Abraham’ (be-Avraham), in his merit, etc.; and it is written: ‘The world shall be built in lovingkindness’ (Psalms 89:3), in lovingkindness, which is the sanctity of the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: For they are all rooted in "the souls that they had gotten in Haran" (Bereishis 12:5), Abraham having spiritually begotten them. And this is what the Sages expounded in Bereishis Rabbah (12:9) on "when they were created" (be-hibar'am): read it b'Avraham ("through Abraham"); he being the primary purpose of the creation of the world, that this soul be formed whence the cosmos unfolds.
column13: And the completion of the structure and the harvest began from Abraham our Father. The explanation of this is found in Midrash Rabbah (9:2): Rabbi Tanchuma expounded: “‘He has made everything beautiful in its time’—in its proper hour the world was created, not being fit to be created prior to that”; Rabbi Abbahu said: This teaches that the Holy One was building worlds and destroying them, until He created these and declared: “This one pleases Me, those did not.”
